hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

assessments.reason: Normal Skype app self-restart with WerFault crash reporting.
PyInstaller implant pushed via PsExec from SCRANTON, spawns powershell and drops Rar/sdelete.
Rar from Temp used by pbeesly to password-encrypt working.zip before wiping.
Anti-forensic wiping of Rar.exe and working.zip on NASHUA.
Azure guest agent log collection, routine.
Sysinternals tool run by attacker PowerShell for permission discovery.
Used by pbeesly with plaintext password to launch python.exe on NASHUA.
Anti-forensic deletion of payload, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip.
Right-to-left-override screen saver launched from explorer that dropped monkey.png stego payload.
C# compiler invoked by hidden PowerShell to build in-memory loader DLLs in Temp.

sdclt abused via DelegateExecute to spawn control.exe and hidden PowerShell.

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network harvested credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access or dumping (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SECURITY hive or NTDS.dit extraction, credential-store access (DPAPI, browser/credential manager files), Kerberoasting/AS-REP roasting, or suspicious access to lsass.exe by non-standard processes.
frame.what_would_refute: No evidence of credential-dumping tooling or LSASS access, no unauthorized reads of SAM/SECURITY/NTDS.dit or credential stores, and no anomalous authentication artifacts consistent with stolen credentials.

verdict.rationale: 5 in-scope incident(s) of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium): I01 T1003.001 (F01, F13, F22, F29, F33, F34, F44, F59), I03 T1056.001 (F55, F56), I04 T1187 (F20), I05 T1552.001 (F26, F57), I07 T1552.004 (F25, F52, F58)
verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Compromised pbeesly session on scranton ran hidden steganography-loaded PowerShell, Sysinternals accesschk/sdelete64 cleanup, certificate private-key export attempts and keystroke/clipboard collection alongside lsass handle access.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 (child of control.exe, hidden -ep bypass loader) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF on scranton at 03:05:16Z; no dump file on disk, but full-access LSASS handles from a non-standard process are consistent with memory credential theft.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM_SERVER 0xF003F handles on SCRANTON, no dump file seen.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds.dit file creation, no ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow execution, no NTDS object access on any host including the DC newyork.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: Only six 4662 queries of Policy\Secrets\$MACHINE.ACC by NT AUTHORITY\LOCAL SERVICE; no lsadump/sekurlsa tooling or SECURITY\Policy\Secrets writes.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: Cache registry writes are TaskCache/NetworkList/AppContainer noise plus normal HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1; no cachedump/mscache/dcc2 commands or SECURITY\Cache object access.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: Single 4662 by the DC's own machine account NEWYORK$ with replication-right GUIDs; no repeated or non-DC replication abuse indicating DCSync.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: No packet-capture driver, promiscuous-mode or raw-socket artifact was observed, but a malicious 'SeaDukeStage' PowerShell stage pushed an unsigned PyInstaller python.exe implant (bundled _socket/_ssl) to NASHUA via PsExec, which then beaconed over TLS to 192.168.0.4:8443 (self-signed cert, Zeek SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert). The implant's network-collection tooling is consistent with network sniffing, but direct capture evidence is absent, so the technique is assessed suspicious rather than confirmed malicious.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Clipboard read and AV check before keylogging.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No Get-Credential or fake GUI prompt code; 'prompt' script blocks are PowerShell module boilerplate.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: Zeek window does not overlap Windows telemetry and the HTTP POST/login check returned zero hits.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: No dumping/hooking code captured, but pbeesly's powershell.exe and wsmprovhost.exe requested full-access (0x1fffff / 0x1f3fff) handles to lsass.exe on scranton and nashua.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 and zero 4771 events in windows.security; only 4776 was a success (0x0). No repeated authentication failures on any host.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: PowerShell 'password' hits are certificate export (pfx password 'saribas') and 7z archive encryption ('lolol'), not login attempts; no password/passwd/pwd command lines in sysmon.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: PowerShell accessed lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff on scranton and exported all LocalMachine certificates, i.e. credential material was obtained, but no cracking tooling, SAM/NTDS dumps or hash files were observed.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: 4648 explicit-credential logons are all for the single account pbeesly, reused against NASHUA over cifs/445 with PSEXESVC.exe on the target - lateral movement, not one-password-many-accounts spraying.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: Only one hardcoded credential pair (cozy / MyCozyPassw0rd!) used once for a WebDAV drive; no stuffing lists and no authentication failures.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smartcard/credential-provider interception artifacts: zero smartcard/NGC/credential-provider file creations, no MFA-related command lines (only the standard NgcSvc svchost host), only standard authentication packages (Kerberos/Negotiate/NTLM) in 4624, CredentialEnrollmentManager registry writes are services.exe creating a built-in per-user service, and the only lsass accesses from PowerShell/wsmprovhost are .NET management-cmdlet queries (0x1000 / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management call trace). The PowerShell 'Credential' hit is a hardcoded-credential WebDAV exfiltration script, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Zeek shows 10.0.1.4 (SCRANTON) forced into WebDAV authentication against 192.168.0.4: DavClnt OPTIONS, rejected SMB probes to 445/139, then Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir OPTIONS/PROPFIND to /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z with an AUTHORIZATION header and 207 Multi-Status responses. A 1 MB 7z lure was uploaded and a 5.3 MB PE (HTTP-FV8BmBzhLupORXNNc.exe) was pulled back, followed on 2020-05-02 by pbeesly Kerberos TGS for cifs/NASHUA and an ADMIN$ PSEXESVC.exe write to nashua.dmevals.local from 10.0.1.4.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: PowerShell (PID 2976) and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff access on scranton and nashua, preceded/followed by a reflective GetProcAddress + base64 PE shellcode loader and hidden encoded PowerShell launched by user pbeesly, plus PsExec with plaintext credentials to NASHUA.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No process read or copied browser cookie/credential stores: sysmon file-create matches for *cookies*/*login data*/*web data*/*local state* yielded only an unrelated LocalService INetCookies file, security 4663 object access on those filenames returned zero rows, and no process-access to browser images was found. The 'cookie' command lines are WebDAV davclnt.dll DavSetCookie calls by pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local pointing at the attacker's 192.168.0.4/webdav exfil share, and Edge file writes are the browser's own profile files — neither is session-cookie theft.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: Password/login-named files archived and encrypted on both hosts.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: Get-ItemPropertyValue 'HKLM:\\SOFTWARE\Javasoft' 'value Supplement' | Invoke-Expression on scranton by pbeesly; no reg query/save of SAM/SECURITY observed.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history, .bash_history or Get-History access found in PowerShell, Sysmon process/file or Security object-access data.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: LocalMachine certs exported to .pfx on SCRANTON.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: No Groups.xml, cpassword or SYSVOL access in PowerShell script blocks, Sysmon process/file events, Security 5145 share access or windows.other messages.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: wsmprovhost full-access lsass handle on NASHUA.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No command lines, file events or object accesses on browser credential stores; only a benign LocalService INetCookies write by svchost.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No vault/cmdkey/credman execution, no registry writes to Vault/Credentials; only a Credential Guard status message.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/.kdbx references in any dataset; the pbeesly PowerShell activity was data staging/exfiltration, not password-manager theft.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Steganographic PowerShell loader (monkey.png) on SCRANTON opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF as pbeesly, followed by PsExec with cleartext credentials to NASHUA — credential access against the auth process, though the process itself was not modified.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: lsass handle opens from PowerShell.exe (0x1FFFFF) and wsmprovhost.exe (0x1F3FFF) indicate targeting of the DC auth process, but all lsass module loads (lsass.exe, samsrv.dll, wdigest.dll) are Microsoft-signed/valid and no SAM/LSA registry changes were seen — no patching evidence.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No Notification Packages/PasswordFilter registry changes, no System32 DLL writes, no password-filter references in PowerShell or other logs.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 events and no AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption/Set-ADAccountControl references in any dataset.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739 (authentication policy change) events in windows.security.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory-service changes and no identity/federation component tampering in image-load data.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: The 36 4657 events are wevtutil Autologger\EventLog-Application config and a SystemCertificates write; no NetworkProvider registration and no unsigned DLLs in winlogon/lsass.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No on-host interception tooling in Windows telemetry; the only AiTM-shaped signal is the zeek L2 duplication of 10.0.1.4 flows, plus an unrelated PsExec-launched C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB/WinRM Kerberos/GSSAPI sessions from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 appear twice with different MAC pairs (00:33 and 00:35), consistent with a relay/interception path; WPAD queries were answered normally and no LLMNR traffic was seen.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: IP 10.0.1.4 is observed on two different source MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) with 44 connections from the second MAC confined to 00:30-00:45, consistent with ARP cache poisoning, though no ARP records or attacker tooling were retrieved.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP server/lease event codes in windows.other, no DHCP-related PowerShell script blocks, and the only ipconfig/netsh/arp/route executions are read-only Azure guest-agent and NetworkWatcher diagnostics on scranton.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: scranton.dmevals.local: malicious PowerShell (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF at 03:05:16 during a confirmed intrusion chain (malicious .scr, C2, persistence, private-key theft) — credential/ticket theft from LSASS is the plausible objective, though no Kerberos-specific tooling was seen.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: krbtgt 4769 requests are AES256 (0x12) TGT requests for pbeesly and SCRANTON$ with Failure Code 0x0, each matched by a 4624 Kerberos logon; no RC4 krbtgt tickets, no 4768/4770/4771, no DCSync/Mimikatz/krbtgt script content.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: All 28 4769 events are AES256 service tickets for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$); no forged service tickets or silver-ticket tooling observed.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: All 4769 tickets use Ticket Encryption Type 0x12 (AES256); no RC4 SPN requests, no GetUserSPNs/Invoke-Kerberoast script blocks, no 4769/4768 in windows.other.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No 4768 AS-REQ events in any dataset and no asreproast/GetNPUsers/Rubeus command lines or script-block content.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential artifacts: no ADFS/SAML/token strings in windows.other or PowerShell 4104, and all 297 4624 logons use standard logon processes (Kerberos/Advapi/User32/NtLmSsp). The hits reflect credential theft (PowerShell->lsass 0x1fffff on scranton) and PSEXESVC lateral movement to NASHUA by pbeesly.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: The 162 *Cookies*/*Login Data*/*Web Data* file-creation hits are svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceState\EventLog\Data\lastalive*.dat; no cookie/SetCookie/document.cookie script blocks and no anomalous logon process indicating cookie replay.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No SAML/NotOnOrAfter/token-signing/ADFS strings in PowerShell or windows.other; lsass accesses are mostly benign 0x1000/0x1400 reads, and the high-privilege ones (PowerShell 0x1fffff on scranton, wsmprovhost 0x1f3fff on nashua) indicate credential dumping rather than token-signing certificate theft.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 4 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's PowerShell (PID 3876) ran a Get-PrivateKeys function that recursively exported every cert:\LocalMachine certificate to a randomly named .pfx in Downloads protected by the hardcoded password "saribas"; Sysmon recorded the resulting C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by that powershell.exe at 2020-05-02T03:04:57Z and touched again at 03:08:51Z. Bulk private-key/certificate theft consistent with T1649; no forged-certificate use or exfiltration observed.

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Returns the current state of the wait for disk resource.

    .PARAMETER DiskNumber
    Specifies the identifier for which disk to wait for.

    .PARAMETER RetryIntervalSec
    Specifies the number of seconds to wait for the disk to become available.

    .PARAMETER RetryCount
    The number of times to loop the retry interval while waiting for the disk.
#>
function Get-TargetResource
{
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([System.Collections.Hashtable])]
    param
    (
        [parameter(Mandatory)]
        [UInt32] $DiskNumber,

        [UInt32] $RetryIntervalSec = 10,

        [UInt32] $RetryCount = 60
    )

    Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
            "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
            $($LocalizedData.GettingWaitForDiskStatusMessage -f $DiskNumber)
        ) -join '' )

    $returnValue = @{
        DiskNumber       = $DiskNumber
        RetryIntervalSec = $RetryIntervalSec
        RetryCount       = $RetryCount
    }
    return $returnValue
} # function Get-TargetResource

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Sets the current state of the wait for disk resource.

    .PARAMETER DiskNumber
    Specifies the identifier for which disk to wait for.

    .PARAMETER RetryIntervalSec
    Specifies the number of seconds to wait for the disk to become available.

    .PARAMETER RetryCount
    The number of times to loop the retry interval while waiting for the disk.
#>
function Set-TargetResource
{
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param
    (
        [parameter(Mandatory)]
        [UInt32] $DiskNumber,

        [UInt32] $RetryIntervalSec = 10,

        [UInt32] $RetryCount = 60
    )

    Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
            "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
            $($LocalizedData.CheckingForDiskMessage -f $DiskNumber)
        ) -join '' )

    $diskFound = $false

    for ($count = 0; $count -lt $RetryCount; $count++)
    {
        $disk = Get-Disk -Number $DiskNumber -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
        if ($disk)
        {
            Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
                    "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
                    $($LocalizedData.DiskFoundMessage -f $DiskNumber,$disk.FriendlyName)
                ) -join '' )

            $diskFound = $true
            break
        }
        else
        {
            Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
                    "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
                    $($LocalizedData.DiskNotFoundMessage -f $DiskNumber,$RetryIntervalSec)
                ) -join '' )

            Start-Sleep -Seconds $RetryIntervalSec
        } # if
    } # for

    if (-not $diskFound)
    {
        New-InvalidOperationException `
            -Message $($LocalizedData.DiskNotFoundAfterError -f $DiskNumber,$RetryCount)
    } # if
} # function Set-TargetResource

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Tests the current state of the wait for disk resource.

    .PARAMETER DiskNumber
    Specifies the identifier for which disk to wait for.

    .PARAMETER RetryIntervalSec
    Specifies the number of seconds to wait for the disk to become available.

    .PARAMETER RetryCount
    The number of times to loop the retry interval while waiting for the disk.
#>
function Test-TargetResource
{
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([System.Boolean])]
    param
    (
        [parameter(Mandatory)]
        [UInt32] $DiskNumber,

        [UInt32] $RetryIntervalSec = 10,

        [UInt32] $RetryCount = 60
    )

    Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
            "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
            $($LocalizedData.CheckingForDiskMessage -f $DiskNumber)
        ) -join '' )

    $disk = Get-Disk -Number $DiskNumber -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
    if ($disk)
    {
        Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
                "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
                $($LocalizedData.DiskFoundMessage -f $DiskNumber,$disk.FriendlyName)
            ) -join '' )

        return $true
    }

    Write-Verbose -Message ( @(
            "$($MyInvocation.MyCommand): "
            $($LocalizedData.DiskNotFoundMessage -f $DiskNumber)
        ) -join '' )

    return $false
} # function Test-TargetResource

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Tests if the current machine is a Nano server.
#>
function Test-IsNanoServer
{
    if (Test-Command -Name Get-ComputerInfo)
    {
        $computerInfo = Get-ComputerInfo

        if ("Server" -eq $computerInfo.OsProductType `
            -and "NanoServer" -eq $computerInfo.OsServerLevel)
        {
            return $true
        }
    }

    return $false
}

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Tests if the the specified command is found.
#>
function Test-Command
{
    param
    (
        [String] $Name
    )

    return ($null -ne (Get-Command -Name $Name -ErrorAction Continue 2> $null))
}

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Creates and throws an invalid argument exception

    .PARAMETER Message
        The message explaining why this error is being thrown

    .PARAMETER ArgumentName
        The name of the invalid argument that is causing this error to be thrown
#>
function New-InvalidArgumentException
{
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param
    (
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [String]
        $Message,

        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [String]
        $ArgumentName
    )

    $argumentException = New-Object -TypeName 'ArgumentException' -ArgumentList @( $Message,
        $ArgumentName )
    $newObjectParams = @{
        TypeName = 'System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord'
        ArgumentList = @( $argumentException, $ArgumentName, 'InvalidArgument', $null )
    }
    $errorRecord = New-Object @newObjectParams

    throw $errorRecord
}

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Creates and throws an invalid operation exception

    .PARAMETER Message
        The message explaining why this error is being thrown

    .PARAMETER ErrorRecord
        The error record containing the exception that is causing this terminating error
#>
function New-InvalidOperationException
{
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param
    (
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [String]
        $Message,

        [ValidateNotNull()]
        [System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord]
        $ErrorRecord
    )

    if ($null -eq $Message)
    {
        $invalidOperationException = New-Object -TypeName 'InvalidOperationException'
    }
    elseif ($null -eq $ErrorRecord)
    {
        $invalidOperationException =
            New-Object -TypeName 'InvalidOperationException' -ArgumentList @( $Message )
    }
    else
    {
        $invalidOperationException =
            New-Object -TypeName 'InvalidOperationException' -ArgumentList @( $Message,
                $ErrorRecord.Exception )
    }

    $newObjectParams = @{
        TypeName = 'System.Management.Automation.ErrorRecord'
        ArgumentList = @( $invalidOperationException.ToString(), 'MachineStateIncorrect',
            'InvalidOperation', $null )
    }
    $errorRecordToThrow = New-Object @newObjectParams
    throw $errorRecordToThrow
}

<#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Retrieves the localized string data based on the machine's culture.
        Falls back to en-US strings if the machine's culture is not supported.

    .PARAMETER ResourceName
        The name of the resource as it appears before '.strings.psd1' of the localized string file.

        For example:
            For WindowsOptionalFeature: MSFT_xWindowsOptionalFeature
            For Service: MSFT_xServiceResource
            For Registry: MSFT_xRegistryResource
#>
function Get-LocalizedData
{
    [CmdletBinding()]
    param
    (
        [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)]
        [ValidateNotNullOrEmpty()]
        [String]
        $ResourceName
    )

    $resourceDirectory = (Join-Path -Path $PSScriptRoot -ChildPath $ResourceName)
    $localizedStringFileLocation = Join-Path -Path $resourceDirectory -ChildPath $PSUICulture

    if (-not (Test-Path -Path $localizedStringFileLocation))
    {
        # Fallback to en-US
        $localizedStringFileLocation = Join-Path -Path $resourceDirectory -ChildPath 'en-US'
    }

    Import-LocalizedData `
        -BindingVariable 'localizedData' `
        -FileName "$ResourceName.strings.psd1" `
        -BaseDirectory $localizedStringFileLocation

    return $localizedData
}

    'New-InvalidOperationException', 'Get-LocalizedData' )

It then repeatedly invoked PsExec64.exe with plaintext credentials (dmevals\pbeesly / Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to launch C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on NASHUA (four launches 03:11:18-03:14:42Z). On nashua.dmevals.local the payload ran as a PyInstaller bundle (extracting _MEI29522 with _socket.pyd/_ssl.pyd/_hashlib.pyd), unsigned (Company/Description '-', IMPHASH all zeros, SHA256 43782EC4337D8F3DDB7EA0C451B3BC4F212F84C8D5571BD0A842001C859A02AE), and opened a rapid burst of TCP connections from 10.0.1.6 to 192.168.0.4:8443 (03:15:05Z onward). Zeek (separate, non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window) shows the same 10.0.1.6 -> 192.168.0.4:8443 pattern as SSL with a self-signed certificate (CN=rempel.group.net) raising an SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert notice, i.e. a covert C2 channel. The implant's bundled _socket/_ssl modules and the 'SeaDukeStage' naming are consistent with a network-collection/sniffing-capable implant, but no packet-capture driver, promiscuous-mode or raw-socket artifact (pktmon, npcap, windump, SIO_RCVALL) was observed in the available telemetry, so the T1040 attribution rests on the implant's network-collection tooling rather than direct capture evidence.

WebDAV forced authentication: SCRANTON (10.0.1.4) sent NTLM credentials to attacker WebDAV server 192.168.0.4
findings.summary: On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:18 and 00:35:25 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (SCRANTON, the same host that later authenticates as pbeesly and pushes PSEXESVC.exe to NASHUA) was driven to authenticate to an external WebDAV server at 192.168.0.4 over HTTP/80. The sequence is textbook forced authentication: first a DavClnt OPTIONS request to '/' (403 Forbidden), then repeated SMB probes to 192.168.0.4 on 445/139 that were all rejected (conn_state REJ), then Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 OPTIONS and PROPFIND requests to /webdav, /webdav/ and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The PROPFIND requests carried an AUTHORIZATION header (client_header_names includes AUTHORIZATION) and returned 207 Multi-Status, i.e. the victim's credentials were accepted by the attacker-controlled server. The lure file OfficeSupplies.7z (1,082,089 bytes, md5 dd5ea7248edbdc4b158e3c81c154857b) was uploaded from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4, and a 5,305,104-byte application/x-dosexec payload was downloaded back from 192.168.0.4 to 10.0.1.4 (extracted as HTTP-FV8BmBzhLupORXNNc.exe). This is the credential-capture step of the intrusion; the Windows datasets (2020-05-02) show the follow-on use of the captured account pbeesly (Kerberos AS/TGS for cifs/NASHUA, ADMIN$ write of PSEXESVC.exe to nashua.dmevals.local from 10.0.1.4).

findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 between 03:01 and 03:21 UTC, user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran PowerShell that opened handles to lsass.exe with credential-dumping-grade access rights: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) requested 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16, and earlier PowerShell.exe (PID 3876) requested 0x1000 at 03:01:03. On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM host spawned by pbeesly's Invoke-Command) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29, with a call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll. At 03:21:29 on scranton, pbeesly's PowerShell created a script block that resolves GetProcAddress/GetModuleHandle via Microsoft.Win32.UnsafeNativeMethods, builds a ReflectedDelegate dynamic assembly and decodes a base64 PE ('/EiD5PDozAAAAEFRQVBSUVZIMdJl...') — an in-memory shellcode/PE loader consistent with exploitation tooling used to reach credential material — plus a second block launching a hidden (-nop -w hidden) gzip/base64 encoded PowerShell payload. The same actor also used PsExec64 with a plaintext password (Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by) to run C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on NASHUA and sdelete64 to wipe files, showing hands-on-keyboard credential abuse. The remaining lsass accesses (svchost.exe, AntimalwareConfig.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, wininit.exe, csrss.exe, services.exe) are normal system/AV behaviour.

findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the user pbeesly ran a hands-on intrusion chain (malicious C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr launched from explorer at 02:55:56, spawning cmd.exe and powershell.exe, then SysinternalsSuite download/extraction, sdelete64 anti-forensics, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Get-PrivateKeys exporting .pfx files, screen capture). At 03:05:16 the same PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — full process access consistent with credential/ticket extraction from LSASS. No Kerberos-specific tooling (Rubeus/Mimikatz/kirbi) was observed in script blocks, so the ticket-theft sub-techniques are not directly evidenced, but the LSASS credential-access prerequisite is clearly present.

On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly (SID S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107) ran a PowerShell session (PID 3876) that defined and invoked a function Get-PrivateKeys. The function enumerates every certificate under cert:\LocalMachine recursively and, for each certificate with a thumbprint, calls Export-PfxCertificate into "$env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\$RandomFileName.pfx" using a hardcoded plaintext password ("saribas"). The script block was recorded at 2020-05-02T03:04:56Z (4104, ScriptBlockId 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) and one second later at 03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by that same powershell.exe (PID 3876). The exported .pfx was touched again by powershell.exe at 03:08:51Z (Sysmon event 23). This is bulk theft of machine certificate private keys with a known export password — exactly the certificate-stealing behaviour of T1649 and a plausible precursor to forging authentication certificates / PKINIT abuse. No Certipy/Certify tooling, no forged-certificate use, and no exfiltration channel for the .pfx were observed in the available windows.

findings.summary: On 2020-05-02, lsass.exe was opened with unusually broad access rights by scripting hosts: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:05:16 requested 0x1FFFFF and 0x1F3FFF, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM host) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29 requested 0x1F3FFF. The remaining rare masks (wininit/csrss 0x1FFFFF at 03:19:09, svchost 0x101001/0x3000) coincide with a boot/reboot sequence on scranton and are consistent with normal system startup. No procdump/comsvcs/MiniDump command line, no 4688 dump process and no lsass-related message in windows.other were found, so a completed LSASS dump is not proven; the PowerShell/WinRM LSASS handles remain unexplained and warrant follow-up on the originating WinRM client.

findings.title: lsass handle access on SCRANTON/NASHUA from PowerShell and wsmprovhost — no DC authentication-process patching observed

The remaining high-access opens (wininit.exe, csrss.exe, svchost.exe 0x101001/0x3000) are normal Windows components. No unsigned or non-Microsoft module was loaded into lsass: the only lsass image loads seen are lsass.exe, samsrv.dll and wdigest.dll, all Signed=true / SignatureStatus=Valid / Signature 'Microsoft Windows'. No 4657 modification of SAM/LSA/Security/Authentication registry keys and no lsass/cryptdll references in other or PowerShell logs. So the DC authentication process was targeted for credential extraction, not patched.

findings.title: Adversary-in-the-Middle: no on-host interception tooling; Temp python.exe launched via PsExec is unrelated to AiTM
findings.summary: On the Windows side (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28) no AiTM tooling was found: the only network-adjacent executions are Azure guest-agent diagnostics (netsh trace, ipconfig /all, arp /a, route print) on scranton.dmevals.local. The most unusual process is C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local, run five times as user pbeesly between 03:11:40 and 03:15:04 with an empty command line, four times parented by C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe and once by itself; this is remote execution of a dropped interpreter, not an interception/relay component, and no evidence ties it to the L2 anomaly seen in the non-overlapping zeek window. The AiTM hypothesis therefore rests on the zeek L2 duplication only; the Windows datasets show no poisoning or relay artifacts.

findings.title: SMB/WinRM authentication traffic to 10.0.1.6 duplicated across two L2 paths; WPAD name resolution present but answered normally
findings.summary: SMB (445) and WinRM (5985) sessions from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 carry Kerberos/GSSAPI authentication (zeek.service 'gssapi,smb,krb') and are recorded twice with different MAC pairs at 00:33:26-00:33:29 and 00:35:25-00:35:26, which is the shape of an SMB/authentication relay or interception path rather than a single direct flow. Name-resolution side: 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 repeatedly query wpad.dmevals.local to the DNS server 10.0.0.4 (8 queries, every 10 minutes) and those queries carry no answers in the retrieved records, so no poisoned WPAD/LLMNR response was observed; the only DNS answers seen are legitimate (newyork.dmevals.local -> 10.0.0.4, wec.dmevals.local -> 10.0.1.10). No LLMNR (5355) traffic appears in the port stack. The relay interpretation rests only on the duplicated L2 paths; no relay tooling, no NTLM relay target and no Windows-side corroboration were retrieved.

findings.title: Same IP 10.0.1.4 observed on two different L2 addresses while talking to 10.0.1.6 (possible ARP cache poisoning / on-path host)
findings.summary: In the zeek window (2020-04-30 00:06-00:45) host 10.0.1.4 normally appears with source MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and its peer 10.0.1.6 with 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69. However 44 connections are recorded with source IP 10.0.1.4 but source MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 and response MAC 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, i.e. the same IP flows appear twice with two different L2 address pairs. The duplicate flows are near-simultaneous: at 00:33:26-00:33:29 WinRM (5985) sessions to 10.0.1.6 are logged once with fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 -> 00:0d:3a:13:e3:69 and once with 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 -> 12:34:56:78:9a:bc, and at 00:35:25-00:35:26 SMB (445) sessions to 10.0.1.6 are likewise duplicated with both MAC pairs. The fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 activity is confined to 00:30-00:45 (4 conns in the 00:30 bucket, 24 in 00:35, 15 in 00:40, 1 in 00:45) and covers 5985, 445, 135 and 55121. This duplicate-IP/differing-MAC pattern is consistent with an on-path host impersonating 10.0.1.4 at layer 2 (ARP cache poisoning) to intercept its SMB/WinRM authentication, but the evidence is indirect: no ARP protocol records, no attacker tooling and no Windows-side corroboration were retrieved, and the zeek window does not overlap the Windows telemetry.

findings.summary: The remaining T1040 check hits are explained by normal system behaviour. No pktmon, windump, tcpdump, rawcap, npcap/WinPcap driver install or promiscuous-mode indicator appeared. findings.title: No brute-force authentication activity; credential theft and reuse instead
findings.summary: Across windows.security (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events and zero 4771 Kerberos pre-auth failures on any of the four hosts (scranton, newyork, nashua, utica). The only 4776 credential validation seen was for pbeesly with status 0x0 (success) on newyork at 03:20:40Z. The only Kerberos error on the wire (zeek, 2020-04-30 window) was KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED (7 events), which is normal pre-authentication negotiation, not an authentication failure. incidents.rationale: All 4648 events involve pbeesly's own credentials to NASHUA via PSEXESVC; no spraying pattern — valid account use, not brute force.

incidents.title: sdclt.exe abused to spawn hidden PowerShell on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: sdclt.exe launched from cmd spawning hidden PowerShell — signed binary proxy execution, not credential access.

incidents.title: hostui.exe launched with runas by PowerShell on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: PowerShell started hostui.exe -verb runas to elevate before the HKLM Javasoft payload — privilege escalation via UAC bypass, not credential access.
